title: From Broad Street to the World: How Newark Built Jersey Club
dek: Before TikTok and the major-label remixes, Jersey club was burned onto CDs and sold on the streets of Newark. Here's how a local sound became a global language.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Every Jersey club track on this station traces back to a handful of Newark DJs at the turn of the millennium. Around 1999 and 2000, DJ Tameil and Tim Dolla began building what they called Brick City club music: a faster, harder take on the Baltimore club records already moving dance floors up and down the East Coast.

Tameil was among the first to make his own tracks. He released the Dat Butt EP on his own label, Anthrax Records, and sold burned CDs on Broad Street. With Mike V and DJ Black Mic, he became part of the Brick Bandits, the crew that did more than anyone to establish the sound in its early years.

The formula is instantly recognisable: roughly 130 to 140 BPM, hard kicks locked into triplet patterns, chopped vocal clips, and the famous bed squeak lifted from Trillville's "Some Cut." It borrowed Baltimore's bounce but carried New Jersey's own history too. This was already house-music country, home to figures like Kerri Chandler and Tony Humphries and to the legendary Newark club Zanzibar.

The scene grew in small rooms, spaces like The Life Lab, where younger Brick Bandits members ran a party called THREAD, and then online, through MySpace, SoundCloud and mix CDs passed hand to hand. DJ Lilman and DJ Frosty made tutorial tracks and videos that taught a generation how to dance to it. By the time DJ Sliink remixed Trey Songz's "Na Na" for Atlantic Records, the major labels had noticed.

body.quote: Jersey club is your morning coffee and your midnight Red Bull.
body.by: UNiiQU3, speaking to The FADER in 2014

body.p: More than a decade later, that description still fits. The names have multiplied and the tempos have climbed, but the DNA laid down on Broad Street is audible in every track on this week's [Rising Now chart](/hot).

title: Viral Before It Was Viral: How Jersey Club Took Over the Internet
dek: TikTok made Jersey club impossible to miss, but the dances and the sound were spreading online long before 2022.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: When Jersey club seemed to be everywhere on TikTok in 2022, it was easy to mistake it for a new trend. It wasn't. The genre had been growing in Newark since the early 2000s, and its dances were already travelling online through Vine and Musical.ly between 2014 and 2018.
Some of the moves going viral today are older than the apps themselves. DJ Lil Man's 2011 track "I Like The Way She Move" introduced dance moves that resurfaced years later as TikTok trends.

body.h2: A beat built for short clips

body.p: Part of the appeal is structural. The bouncing kick patterns and signature sounds, like the bed squeak and the five-count kick, read instantly in a few seconds of video. Those same elements have since turned up in mainstream records such as Drake's "Massive."
The sound also opened doors for rappers. Newark's Bandmanrill built his career on Jersey club production:

body.quote: I only started rapping over Jersey Club beats because I wanted to be different.

body.p: Behind the scenes, collectives like Project X, a Jersey-based crew of producers, dancers and artists, and figures like producer and radio host DJ Lil Taj kept the culture rooted at home while the rest of the world caught on.
The tipping point was Lil Uzi Vert's "Just Wanna Rock" in October 2022, co-produced by 19-year-old Newark producer MCVertt. [Read the full story](/news/just-wanna-rock-mcvertt).
The pattern hasn't stopped. This week's [Rising Now chart](/hot) is full of flips and remixes spreading the same way: clip by clip.

title: UNIIQU3 Keeps Flipping Jersey Club's Past Into Its Future
dek: Newark's Jersey Club Queen went from classically trained pianist to an international touring DJ. Her secret weapon is the sample.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Few artists have done more to carry Jersey club beyond Newark than UNIIQU3. She came up in the city's club scene in the early 2010s with an unusual foundation: classical piano. She learned production and sampling on a keyboard, and that musicianship still shapes how she builds a track.

Her 2018 single "Microdosing" was a breakout, and the same year she co-created "Off the Chain" with TT The Artist, produced by Mighty Mark. Since then she has remixed artists including Chloe Bailey and Aluna George (her Jersey club remix featured in Chloe Bailey's Coachella performance), toured with Tinashe, and curated the TECHNO IS BLACK playlist on Spotify. She performs regularly across North America, Europe and Asia.

In 2024 she appeared in Serato's Hometown Sounds series alongside Just Blaze and Rah Digga, flipping Rah Digga's "Party & Bullshit 2003," a Just Blaze production, into Jersey club. Her tools are modern, including Serato Sample and its stem-separation technology, but the instinct is pure club: find the moment in a record that moves a room.

body.quote: It's just so dope to be behind the decks and have everybody in unison for that one moment.
body.by: UNIIQU3, speaking to The FADER in 2024

body.p: A decade earlier she summed up the genre as "your morning coffee and your midnight Red Bull." She's still the one pouring it. Hear where the next generation is taking the sound on [Rising Now](/hot).

title: Labs, Club Noise and 180 BPM: Where Jersey Club Goes Next
dek: Two decades in, Jersey club is still mutating. These are the traditions and sub-styles pushing it forward.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Jersey club started out as Brick City club in Newark in the early 2000s, a local adaptation of the Baltimore club sound. More than twenty years later it is less a single style than a family of them.

The core is still recognisable: bass-heavy 808 triplet drums synchronised with gun clicks and squeaky-bed samples, usually hovering around 130 BPM. Pioneers like DJ Tameil, whose early releases on his own Anthrax Records label helped set the template, and crews like the Brick Bandits laid that foundation.

The Brick Bandits also helped seed a wave of Jersey club supergroups, among them Project X, Twerknation28, 4KAE and Anthem Gxds. Today's scene spans names like UNIIQU3, DJ Sliink, R3LL, Andy pls and MANIIA.

One of the newest traditions is the "lab," short for collab, where several producers each contribute their own section to a single track. It's a format built for a community where everyone brings a signature sound.
Tempos are climbing too. Newer variants run as fast as 170 to 180 BPM, and a sub-style called #ClubNoise, founded by markds, pushes distorted 808s and fast, sharp chopping.

body.quote: Jersey Club is that bass you feel in your chest the second it hits.

body.p: You can hear the family tree growing in real time: this week's [Rising Now chart](/hot) is full of fresh flips, remixes and labs uploaded in just the last few weeks.

title: Tang, Drill and the Dance Floor: The Movement Behind Jersey Club
dek: Jersey club has always been dance music first. Its offshoots and dance styles are how it keeps spreading.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Jersey club has always been measured by what it does to a room. Born in Newark in the early 2000s as a local twist on the Baltimore club sound, it was built at 130 to 140 BPM for dancing, not background listening.
In the mid-2010s a darker branch appeared. Jersey drill carried Chicago drill influences into the club template, keeping the bounce while changing the mood.

The Tang dance originated in Philadelphia but became closely tied to Jersey club. It's built on expressive arm movements that mimic boxing or flexing, and it's often performed battle-style. In the 2020s it went viral on TikTok, carrying the sound to audiences who had never heard of Newark.

That's the pattern throughout the genre's history: underground parties first, then MySpace, SoundCloud and mix CDs, then viral platforms. Each wave brought new dancers, and the dancers brought new listeners, right up to Lil Uzi Vert's 2022 hit "Just Wanna Rock," produced by Newark's MCVertt. [Read the story behind it](/news/just-wanna-rock-mcvertt).
Want to know what the dance floor is moving to right now? This week's [Rising Now chart](/hot) tracks the Jersey club uploads gaining the most plays.

title: Two Minutes That Changed Jersey Club: "Just Wanna Rock" and MCVertt
dek: Lil Uzi Vert's 2022 single wasn't a rap song or a rock song. It was Jersey club, co-produced by a teenager from Newark.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: In October 2022, Lil Uzi Vert released "Just Wanna Rock," the lead single from the album that became Pink Tape (2023). The song had already built huge momentum on TikTok, where Uzi teased it before release.
Stereogum summed up the surprise in one line:

body.quote: Uzi has gone full Jersey club on this one.

body.p: At roughly two minutes long, the track runs on rhythm and movement rather than verses, which made it tailor-made for dance videos.

The beat came from Synthetic, who had previously worked with Yeat, and MCVertt, a 19-year-old Jersey club producer from Newark and a member of Project X, the Jersey-based collective of producers, dancers and artists.

"Just Wanna Rock" peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100. By Complex's count in December 2022 it had passed 70 million Spotify streams, with 17 million views on its video. More importantly, it showed the mainstream what Newark had known for twenty years.
The sound has kept moving since. Hear this week's fastest-rising Jersey club tracks on [Rising Now](/hot).
